newsitem.title: USA: U.S. floods hit casinos, strand tourists.
newsitem.headline: U.S. floods hit casinos, strand tourists.

text.p: Hundreds of people were flooded out of their homes, gambling casinos were sandbagged and 2,300 people were stranded in Yosemite National Park as relentless rain pounded the western United States on Thursday.
Pacific storms, which have caused havoc in Washington state and Oregon for the last week, hammered California, Nevada and Idaho, leaving a trail of floods, mudslides, power outages and closed roads.

Several hundred evacuees spent Wednesday night in shelters in northern California's wine country, where the Russian and Napa rivers broke their banks, flooding the town of Guerneville and inundating vineyards.

In Nevada, heavy rain caused the worst flooding in downtown Reno in more than 40 years. Several hotel-casinos in the Reno area closed and moved their clients to other hotels. Other casinos remained open but were sandbagged. Reno International Airport was closed.

Gov. Bob Miller declared a state of emergency in four Nevada counties while Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber declared emergencies in five storm-hit counties and mobilized 200 National Guard troops to help with transportation, traffic control and sandbagging. Gov. Mike Lowry has declared a state of emergency in 19 Washington counties.
At least 14 deaths are blamed on the storms, estimated to have caused up to $250 million in property damage in Washington, Oregon and northern California.

Three hikers missing in the Mount Shasta area of northern California were found alive and well on Thursday, the Siskiyou County Sheriff's Department said. The search continued for another three hikers missing in Snohomish County northeast of Seattle.
About 2,300 tourists, park workers and their families were stranded in California's scenic Yosemite National Park, 150 miles (240 km) southeast of San Francisco, officials said.
Heavy rain pushed the Merced River over its banks, closing all highways into Yosemite Valley, where the park headquarters and accommodation are located, they said.

Park spokesman Kendell Thompson said there were about 1,100 tourists in Yosemite Valley and about 1,200 staff and their families. Rooms were available for all the guests and park employees had homes in the valley, he said.
"They are warm and dry. There is enough food. The electricity is still on. Everybody is in good shape," he said. He said it was a "top priority" to find a way to evacuate people from the park.

Alister Bull, a Reuters correspondent vacationing in the park, said he had been planning to leave Yosemite on Thursday but was prevented from doing so because the roads were under water and closed. "We are literally marooned. There is three feet of water across the road on both sides of us," he said.

Bull said guests were handed a park bulletin stating that the National Parks Service was planning an emergency air evacuation of all guests from Yosemite Valley. It said evacuation may be necessary "due to a complete failure of Yosemite Valley sewer system." However, a park spokeswoman said bad weather had ruled out an air evacuation for now.
In northern California's wine country, the Russian River burst its banks, inundating homes and businesses in Guerneville, 50 miles (80 kms) north of San Francisco.
A flood watch was issued for the Pajaro River in central California which rose quickly because of heavy rain.

About 19,000 homes and business in northern and central California were without electricity because of the storm and about 13,600 customers remained cut off in the Seattle area, utility officials said.

In Seattle, mudslides forced the evacuation of more than 40 homes -- many valued at well over $1 million -- overlooking Puget Sound in the city's exclusive Magnolia section. Several homes sustained serious damage.
In Oregon, floodwaters shut off access to downtown Tualatin south of Portland, and the posh suburb of Lake Oswego, hard hit by a flood last February, once again was threatened by rising waters.
